title: AES encryption
summary: AES is a specification for encrypting electronic data established by NIST, adopted as a FIPS standard in 2001. It is a symmetric-key block cipher based on a substitution–permutation network, operating on 128-bit blocks with key sizes of 128, 192, or 256 bits. The number of processing rounds is 10, 12, or 14 respectively. Each round applies SubBytes (byte substitution using a lookup table), ShiftRows (row-wise cyclic shifting), MixColumns (column-wise linear mixing), and AddRoundKey (XOR with a derived round key). The key schedule expands the cipher key into round keys. Decryption uses inverse operations. AES superseded DES and is used by the US government; it is the only publicly accessible cipher approved by NSA for top-secret information when used in an approved module.

mechanisms.title: SubBytes
mechanisms.explanation: Each byte in the state array is replaced using a fixed 8-bit lookup table (S-box). The S-box is derived from the multiplicative inverse in GF(2^8) combined with an invertible affine transformation, providing non-linearity and avoiding algebraic attacks.

mechanisms.title: Key Expansion
mechanisms.explanation: The cipher key is expanded into a series of round keys using the AES key schedule. A separate 128-bit round key block is generated for each round plus one additional key, which is XORed with the state during the AddRoundKey step.
